speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house for a minute or two to perform a unique but very pleasant duty on behalf of my good friend Dr. L. E. Borden, who was surgeon and botanist with the first dominion government expedition to the Arctic, 1903-04. I cannot do better to inform the house on this question than to read Dr. Borden's letter accompanying the proclamation signed by Commander Low when he took possession of Ellesmere land and adjacent islands in the name of Canada. It reads:
To the honourable members of the House of Commons, Ottawa, Canada.
From Dr. L. E. Borden,
1315 Monterey Avenue, Victoria, B.C.
Sir:
I have the honour to present to you for your consideration this important document.
I have always felt that the permanent home of this proclamation in my possession should be the dominion archives. As it has now served its purpose as far as I am personally concerned, I have much pleasure in handing it over to its proper resting place.
This copy was made in my presence on board the D.G.S. Neptune, as was the copy that was placed in the cairn on Ellesmere land. My copy has reposed in my diary ever since and very few people have seen it. When I produced it for Mr. H. W. Herridge to see, he was a very much surprised man. As far as I know this is the only copy in existence, and is an irreplaceable proclamation.
I may at some future date give my original diary to the dominion archives as well.
L. E. Borden.
I take much pleasure, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of Dr. Borden in presenting this proclamation to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys so it may be placed in the archives of Canada.

I understood, sir, I was to get answers to a couple of questions and that was the only reason this item was stood. I was asked by the hon. member for Prince Albert to give the number of applications for citizenship which had been rejected. I asked him to be a little more specific about that and it was finally understood, I think, that I would give definitely the number that had been rejected by the minister in the year 1955 after being recommended by a judge. I had a count made and the number was 162. I found also that it was possible without very great difficulty to go through the


files and make a count of those applications which were rejected by the courts, that is to say where the applications came in and the judge had not seen fit to recommend them. There were 85 of those, so that the total number of rejections was 247. I gave the figure the other night of the number granted and that was 58,715.

The
information which the minister has given to the house this morning establishes one thing quite definitely, and that is that he accepts, and has accepted in given instances, the responsibility for examining citizenship applications which have been recommended by a judge and, with the authority given to him by the statute, of disagreeing with the judge, reversing the judge's findings by refusing to grant citizenship. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that is, in itself, largely in disagreement with the attitude taken by the minister when this point was first debated in this house, at which time he indicated he felt he was practically bound by the findings-

I do not think we should proceed along this line any further. I indicated very clearly on three separate occasions the other evening that these applications came to the minister with a recommendation from a judge. It was the duty of the minister to exercise his discretion, but in the exercise of his discretion it had never been the practice to look into what was done in the courts and try to review the work in the courts. I have looked back to see what my hon. friend the Minister of Finance said when the amendment was made two or three years ago, and I find that his view then was the same as the position I am taking now. What we do is to see if we have detrimental information, and I said this quite clearly the other night, in the citizenship branch or elsewhere in the department that is not available to the courts. We do not attempt to review what takes place in the courts, or to sit as a superior court over the courts. I think it would be quite improper if that were done.

Be
that as it may, we have the situation in which the minister says, "I do not attempt to review what has gone through our citizenship courts". And then we find that subsequently he sees fit to reverse 162 of those recommendations. To me, that is a clear-cut indication that in certain cases, for whatever reason, he chooses to reverse the findings of the citizenship court.

It is not a question of reversing at all. I wish the hon. gentleman

would use the proper terms as they are used in the act. There is a recommendation and the recommendation is accepted or it is not. There is no reversing of anything.

agree with the minister that he refused to go along with the recommendation of the citizenship court. I am prepared to accept that.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we will all remember from the evidence introduced when this item was last debated it was apparent that this citizenship application went through with the minimum of delay

That, sir, is not true, either. This application was considered on April 16 and the certificate was not signed until April 28. I could give many instances where it had been done much more quickly than that, several times at the request of certain hon. gentlemen opposite.

One
asks oneself-at least I certainly do-why this citizenship application should have been processed with such speed because the minister will, I think, agree with me that while other applications may have been processed speedily, this application was processed much more speedily than the average in the department.
I do not think, sir, the average is much more than 12 days.

In
that case, Mr. Chairman, it indicates that the average application in the citizenship department is being processed and citizenship papers put out on a Saturday morning. Since an average represents 50 per cent of the work, we have the peculiar situation in which the minister's department is doing most of its work on a Saturday morning, and he himself knows how foolish that is.
I do more work on Saturdays than on most other days every week in the year.

question why this application was handled so expediently and so successfully in the light of certain questions regarding it. One wonders how this could be done. in a position to obtain this particular type of treatment. Let me make a further point, Mr. Chairman, because it has been somewhat obscure in newspaper reports in the last two or three days.
What is at issue here is not a question of a private quarrel between a mother and her daughter over an estate valued at several million dollars; what is at issue here is the procedure followed by this department in granting the most treasured possession which Canadians can have, their citizenship.
It is important that we take a stand on whether citizenship is going to be granted to those who will value and cherish it and use it here in Canada or whether it is going to be granted to someone who in this case is going to wear it on the shoulder of her dress like a little badge and show that badge practically all the time outside of Canada, refusing to live in Canada and follow the normal procedure of a Canadian citizen in that respect.
I suggest to the committee, Mr. Chairman, that it has been conclusively proven that during the last year when the act called for the applicant to reside continuously in Canada her residence here was of a very short duration. The evidence would indicate that actually it was in the nature of two weeks to a month during that entire year.
The evidence would indicate further that in the preceding years at which time the act also called for the applicant to reside in Canada for four out of a preceding six years, her residence in Canada was of a very temporary nature if indeed it can be said that
7436	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration there was any residence here. We also know that this woman's minor children have lived continuously in Europe and that no attempt has been made to establish their residence in Canada. We know, too, that immediately upon obtaining her Canadian citizenship this lady left for Europe and has remained there almost continuously since and that at the present time she is, to quote the words of her lawyer in New York, "on tour in Europe". I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, she is hardly the type of person who is going to take a great interest in her Canadian citizenship.
Regarding the star chamber proceedings of this court in Montreal, let us remind ourselves that those who opposed her application offered to supply stenographers to take down the evidence and were refused.

Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps the hon. gentleman is as ignorant of the proceedings in these courts and the proceedings that have been carried on in all these cases everywhere as he appears to be of most of the true facts of this particular case in other respects.
I might point out that it is not the custom to carry on these inquiries in public in any case. The judge receives the applicant in his chambers and asks questions in order to determine whether the person is a suitable individual to receive citizenship. Some of these questions are of an extremely personal nature and I know of no case-I have never heard of any case since I became minister- where these inquiries have been held in public. I think it would be a very undesirable and retrograde step if they were to be held in public.
There is, as the hon. member for Cartier pointed out, a provision in the act for any person who wishes to oppose one of these applications to make representations in writing. Certain representations were made in this case and I am informed were considered. It was proceeded with in the same way as in any other case and the use of terms like "star chamber" is quite inappropriate and a misrepresentation of what really happened.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I draw the hon. member's attention to the provisions of citation 253 of Beauchesne's third edition which reads in part as follows:
All reference to judges and courts of justice and to personages of high official station, of the nature of personal attack and censure, have always been considered unparliamentary-
I hope the hon. member will remember that citation in his reference to this particular court.

The
minister went to great length to point out to us recently that this court is not of exactly


the same nature as a court of law. That was given as one of the reasons why they refused to permit the opposant to be present at the time of the hearing.

That is not a correct statement either. The only difference between this court and any other court that acts in matters of citizenship is that the clerk and other officials of the court are federal civil servants instead of being provincial civil servants, but the judge is appointed by the federal government as is the case with county court and superior court judges. I was indicted with great warmth the other day by the hon. member for Kamloops when he said I was contemptuous of the courts in connection with immigration matters, a statement that was completely untrue. He made a great deal of the allegation that I paid no attention to the courts and disregarded the courts. Now the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace comes here and says that I should set myself up above the courts and review their proceedings and interfere with what happens in the courts. I say that that is a shocking suggestion for any hon. member to make.

The
minister says it is shocking but he did it 162 times last year.

That is completely and unreservedly false; I did not do that in any single case. When I receive a recommendation, in every case I consider our own records in the department and such other records as are available to us and any other information that is available and relevant, but we never look at the proceedings in the courts. We assume that the judge has done his duty properly and that what he has done is not for us to review.

can only draw hon. members' attention to the words in Hansard where the minister pointed out that in the past year he had rejected 162 applications which had been recommended to him by a judge of one of these courts, and that shortly afterward he said that he did not act as a court of appeal. He claims such action would be simply a shocking thing. I leave it to the committee to decide what is correct and what is not correct in the minister's statement.
However, I am not attacking the judiciary or the courts; I am pointing out certain facts in order to proceed one step further and bring forward certain other interesting facts which have since come to my attention in connection with this case. I was pointing out at the time of the minister's original interruption that despite the fact the opposant offered

to supply the proper stenographic assistance to transcribe the proceedings, that was refused by the court. Subsequently the hearings were held in chambers with the opposant and attorney for the opposant excluded. I shall not labour the business of the exclusion. The minister told us a few moments ago that to all intents and purposes this was a court. I suggest to you therefore that it is highly improper, in the light of his own statement that this is a court, that the completely traditional procedure of having attorneys for the opposants present at every stage of the proceedings should have been thrown overboard in this particular case. It leads us, however, to certain difficulties in assessing the evidence on which the minister presumably came to a conclusion because we find that the findings of the president of the court of Canadian citizenship, Paul Fontaine, on April 16, 1956 include the following. He refers to a certain time when the petitioner was in Brazil and then he continues:
From there she went to the United States where she stayed until November, 1950, at which time she came to Canada.
That is quite a statement, a very definite statement of residence on the part of this applicant in the United States. On the other hand, we find the same applicant on the 21st day of May, 1956, in a sworn statement which, incidentally, was also made in Rome, Italy, referring to her United States residence and denying it. There was a question of guardianship and her location in connection with that. This is the signed and sworn statement by the same person who was said by the judge of the court to have stayed in the United States:
With reference to such guardianship, it is true that deponent had a mailing address at 55 West 55th street, but neither petitioner nor deponent ever lived there. Annexed to this affidavit is the affidavit of Seymour Groshut, Esq., a member of the New York Bar and the president of New York Associates, Inc., the owner since 1943 of the premises located at 55 west 55th street.
As appears from said affidavit, the apartment in question was occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Ajo, their daughter and a governess. It consisted of four rooms, a kitchen, livingroom and two bedrooms. Neither deponent nor petitioner ever spent a night in that apartment. During this period, deponent's recollection is that she visited New York on not more than two occasions (petitioner not at all), and stayed for not more than two or three days. On no occasion did deponent stop elsewhere than at a hotel, the Langdon as deponent believes. Petitioner well knows that neither she nor deponent was domiciled in New York during the period in question. . . .
We have there, Mr. Chairman, what would seem to me to be evidence given to the judge-

gave it a moment ago. It is dated May 21, 1956 and it was executed in the province of Rome, city of Rome, embassy of the United States of America. It was sworn to before the vice-consul of the United States of America.

I should like to know how the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or the judge of the court could have been expected in April to know the contents of a document that did not exist until May and then was prepared in Rome.

The
point I am making is that the minister rushed this application through with such expediency-
I presume the hon. member means expedition.

-.
that it was not properly dealt with and all the facts were not brought out. The house will remember that I drew attention to a telegram from the attorney for the opposition dated May 24, 1956 stating that he had certain facts that he thought should be produced to the minister and the minister refused to accept those facts and told the attorney that if he wished to proceed on the basis of them he should go to the courts himself.
Another document in connection with the case which is interesting is one which I hold in my hand, and to refresh the memory of hon. members I should like to refer to the findings of the judge in Montreal regarding residence on this lady's yacht. His findings read in part as follows:
From April 25, 1955, to December 3, 1955, the petitioner lived aboard a yacht owned by the Merida Co., an incorporated company under the laws of the province of Quebec flying British and Canadian merchant marine flags.
The date I would underline in that connection is April 25, 1955 because again I hold in my hand a document, the authenticity of which is sworn to before Mr. Pierre Dupuis in the Canadian embassy at Rome. The document is in Italian and I will therefore not attempt to read it. But it is the commissioning papers of this particular yacht on which the lady claims to have lived from April 25, 1955, and it is interesting that the yacht was commissioned on the 1st of July, 1955, a month and a week after she claimed to have taken up residence on the yacht. Incidentally, the document also indicates that the commission of the yacht expired at the end of August. It is quite possible that the commission may
7438	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration have been renewed subsequently to cover her residence on the yacht until December 3, but there seems to be very grave doubt that the yacht was even in the water until the end of June, 1955. There has been some indication that the yacht was in the shipyards during the early part of the period that Madame Feltrinelli claims residence thereon.
I would point out just in passing that the registry of the yacht is actually British and not Canadian, although it is owned in Canada.
So much time for one case.

There is one other point I should like to bring up. Earlier in the debate the Minister of Trade and Commerce rose to his feet in the house, innocence dripping from him like water from a lake Ontario swimmer, and said in effect: "What is this all about? The rest of us should know something about this." Then he asked me a string of questions. That was three or four days ago. I drew to the minister's attention at that time that he had received letters and copies of letters to the Minister of Justice outlining the details of the case, but I was not aware at that time that another letter also was in existence. It is on the letterhead of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is dated May 7, 1956 and reads:
I wish to acknowledge receipt of your letter of May 4, and copies of your correspondence with the Hon. Stuart Garson, Minister of Justice, and the office of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in connection with the application for naturalization of Mrs. Giovanna Feltrinelli. I appreciate having this information in the event that I am consulted in this case.
The letter is signed "C. D. Howe". I draw that to the attention of the house to indicate the cavalier attitude which has been adopted towards the case by various members of the government who wrote acknowledging receipt of the details and then when they came into the house claimed that they knew nothing about it. There are on file a goodly number of other letters acknowledging receipt of this material from such people as the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Transport, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Secretary of State. By the way, if I may stop at this point, the Secretary of State writes: Dear Mr. Levitsky:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter of May 4, with its enclosures, concerning the application for naturalization of Mrs. Giovanna Feltrinelli, which I shall discuss with my colleagues.
I am just wondering what the results of that discussion may have been. The Minister of Labour also acknowledged receipt of the material. The Minister of Fisheries also acknowledged receipt of this material.
They were very courteous.

On
behalf of the Prime Minister, it is acknowledged by Mr. J. S. Cross, his secretary; and on behalf of certain other ministers it is acknowledged by people in their office, such as the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the Solicitor General and the Minister of Veterans Affairs. However, I would specifically point out to the house that the first batch of letters to which I drew attention were acknowledged and signed by the particular ministers. Hence the cabinet can hardly claim that they knew nothing about this particular case.
I do not propose to pursue this matter any further, although if one wished to do so, as the house can see from the various evidence that has been produced, one could make a case which, going beyond this into other detail which is available, would be even stronger. However, I do not feel that there is any point, once you build an impregnable stone wall, in continuing to pile stones on top. This case is so clear and so definite that I will try to conclude by restating the three principal points.
Time!

The
first point is the conduct of the citizenship court in Montreal in this most unusual case where an application is being opposed-that is unusual procedure and it makes it an unusual application-I refer to their conduct in refusing to allow the opposant's attorneys to hear the evidence being given on behalf of the applicant or to have a transcript made of that evidence so that they might be in a position to examine it in detail and to assist the court in arriving at its findings. The second point is the rather amazing expediency and speed with which this particular case was handled. While I cannot give any reason as to why these things may have happened, I know that if I have anyone who has a particularly difficult case of application for citizenship and they are wondering to whom to go, I will certainly recommend the Prime Minister's nephew.
I suggest that you recommend the hon. member for York West who wrote to me about a somewhat similar case and who received a very courteous and prompt reply.

Having established those two facts, Mr. Chairman, we come to the question of this woman's evident lack of desire and lack of intention to live in Canada. That more than anything else is the thing which bothers me in this

case, namely that this lady had not lived in Canada prior to getting her Canadian citizenship, that she is not living here now and that there seems to be no indication whatsoever that she plans to live in Canada. I suggest that it is an improper thing for citizenship to be granted to someone who does not expect to assume as a Canadian citizen the responsibilities of residence here in this country.
Then finally we come to the question of this evidence which I have introduced to the house this morning in connection with a couple of things and certain other evidence which the minister brushed off and personally refused to see, at the same time directing the person who had this evidence to make it his own private case in the courts of Quebec. The minister, having given the woman Canadian citizenship, apparently refused to have anything further to do with the matter and washed his hands of it, despite the well-known fact that it is possible for him to revoke his action. That is the case, Mr. Chairman. It is clear-cut. Would the minister care to answer one question in order to help me?
Time!

Who
signed the letter which is in the Feltrinelli file which came from Montreal to Ottawa, which urged particularly fast action on this case before the opposant took certain court proceedings which might prevent the issuance of the naturalization certificate and which I believe was directed to the minister himself?

Yes, Mr. Chairman; I should be delighted to answer that question. That assertion was made to me and I had the files searched. Not content with that, I searched the files myself and I was unable to find any such letter.

There was a question as to how many Chardin paintings there were which were not identical with but similar to the one that was acquired in the group of four paintings quite recently. I am told that so far as is known there were four. The one belonging to the national gallery was formerly in the collection of the Prince of 67509-472

The picture itself is dated 1739. It is rather thought to be the first of them, although there is no absolute proof of that. But there is one in the Louvre, as the hon. gentleman has said; and the fact that there is one in the Louvre is of some comfort to the board of trustees of the national gallery. Then the hon. gentleman asked me about the storage building on Echo drive. I think I cannot add to the answer I gave. I was fairly sure that my answer was right.
Then the hon. gentleman also asked about the war record pictures. I am told that the national gallery does not own them but that it has custody of them.
Then the final question was about these paintings belonging to Professor Bangarth. I am told that on June 22, 1954, Professor Bangarth showed the then director, Dr. McCurry, a painting attributed to Rembrandt, "Portrait of Rembrandt's Mother" and "Interior of an Inn" by David Teniers. I hope that is the right pronunciation. My Dutch is not too good, althought I had Dutch ancestors. The file records the director's remarks: "These are not anything we want to enter into discussion about".
On August 11, 1955 the director was approached-that is the present director-by a Mr. Kingsley Jarvis of Norris, Allen Limited, of Toronto, who offered to show the national gallery four pictures: a Rembrandt, a Tiepolo, a Teniers and a Modigliani. The director replied on August 16 that the gallery would be interested in these pictures if the asking price was in line with present market values, and also if the paintings were of the quality of the notes which Mr. Kingsley Jarvis submitted would suggest. I am putting in the given names of these Jarvises so as to avoid as much confusion as I can.
Then, Mr. Kingsley Jarvis replied on August 17 saying the four paintings were then being offered to some other collector but enclosing photographs of two of them. The research department of the gallery recognized those pictures as belonging to Professor Bangarth, and pictures that had already been drawn to their attention. They came to the conclusion from an examination of the photographs and the other evidence that these were not pictures in which the gallery would be interested. I am told that the normal practice is for the gallery, when pictures are offered, to ask to have photographs submitted, to subject them to very
7440	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration careful scrutiny by experts in the gallery, and if that scrutiny reveals them to be of real interest, then they ask to have the picture itself sent to the gallery at the expense of the gallery for examination. But if they feel there is no real interest and the board would not be likely to buy them, they do not believe it is proper to use the funds of the gallery for this purpose.
Now, there may be one or two other pictures in this collection of Professor Bangarth's of which the gallery has not had photographs, and if there are they would be very glad to examine the photographs and follow the usual procedure. I have no doubt that if Professor Bangarth wanted to bring the pictures to Ottawa himself at his own expense, they would be glad to examine them. I think the hon. gentleman asked me what officials had examined them, and since this is a matter of expertise, I have no hesitation in giving the names of the officials. I would not pretend to take anything but a ministerial responsibility because I am not an expert on pictures. They were Dr. Hubbard and Dr. Dale, both of whom I think are known to the hon. member, and both of whom are doctors of the fine arts.

I am very pleased to hear the answer the minister has given. It answers a number of questions I had in mind regarding these Tillsonburg pictures. I am informed by a letter here that the gallery had seen the actual picture which was purported to be a Rembrandt, as the minister said, and also one by Teniers. Professor Bangarth has a number of other pictures, including a Titian, a Degoya and a number of others. I am assured again, by a letter received the day before yesterday, that these pictures are genuine and he can prove that they are. As the minister knows, I like him am not an expert and I would not know whether or not they were originals.
In view of the fact that these claims are made and apparently in the past they have been represented to the minister by responsible people, I do feel that a glance at a photograph of a picture would hardly be sufficient. I think most hon. members would realize that there is enough controversy very often over pictures, as to whether they are genuine, when people examine the actual pictures carefully, the kind of paint used and that sort of thing. A photograph would hardly be sufficient. The minister has said, as I understand it, that if Professor Bangarth wishes to bring these pictures to the gallery they will be examined.

I have no doubt whatever that would be done. I think the hon. gentleman would agree that we could hardly use


the taxpayers' money to have them brought here unless the gallery was practically certain it was genuinely interested and that the seller would, under the circumstances, have to bear the cost of making the pictures available for inspection. They would certainly be inspected. Of that, I have not the slightest doubt whatever, and inspected by the best expert they have.

I have just one further remark. I am inclined to agree with the minister but I would think possibly, in view of the fact that Professor Bangarth claims these pictures are genuine and if they are they are of obvious value to the gallery, and since it is a very costly and risky thing to transport pictures of this type around the country, perhaps in the near future Mr. Alan Jarvis or some other member of the gallery would be in Toronto and might go over to Tillsonburg to see these pictures. It is not a great distance and perhaps it would be possible for the minister to agree to that.

I do not think I should like to commit other people to go to Tillsonburg. It would give me the greatest pleasure to go up to Tillsonburg at any time because, as the hon. gentleman knows, I have special reasons for liking to go to that neighbourhood whenever I can find an excuse for it. I will draw it to the attention of the director, and I am sure he will do whatever is reasonable.
Item agreed to.
179.	Departmental administration, $702,905.

Mr. Chairman, these estimates were before the estimates committee on April 18 where I made a statement regarding the Department of Labour estimates proper. Then, on August 2 a statement was made by the chief commissioner with regard to the unemployment insurance commission. In addition to that, discussions were held in the estimates committee over quite a long period of time. On June 14 I made quite a long statement and for a full day these estimates were discussed in the house.

Item agreed to.
180.	To provide for expenses of the economics and research branch, $547,762.

In connection with this particular item, this morning I could not help but hear over the C.B.C. news that Dr. Cyril James of McGill University made an announcement. I am sorry that I did not have facilities at the moment to take down exactly what the announcement said, but as I recall, it was to the effect that Dr. Cyril James announced that at a meeting recently held the

various heads of universities had discussed this question of training engineers and technicians. As a result of this conference the heads of the various universities estimated that the number of engineers and scientists being turned out by all the universities and technical schools in the United States and in the free world put together were just about equal to one-half of the scientists and engineers being trained in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
As I recall the bulletin, Dr. James apparently said that a further meeting would be held later in the year to discuss this question of training engineers and scientists.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Order.
There is one thing that is quite clear to me, Mr. Chairman. We have heard this matter discussed repeatedly in this house on several occasions and under other headings.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Order.
If the senior member for Halifax would keep still-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I will rise on a point of order, and I should like the hon. member to indicate how what he is saying is in any way related to the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour.
I should like very much to answer. It is the item under which this whole question was discussed in the committee and in the house, and the hon. member is certainly quite in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member for Halifax would care to wait a minute I, as chairman, would like to have some assistance from the Minister of Labour because I am not informed about this item.

The topic which my hon. friend is approaching now comes under several items in my estimates, some under labour and some under unemployment insurance. I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton West that under item 180, to provide for expenses of the economics and research branch, part of the duties of that branch is to carry out a study of manpower, womanpower and personnel for employment in Canada; whereas under the Unemployment Insurance Act and the national employment service comes more directly the role of assisting those people in the finding of employment.
While I am on my feet, perhaps my hon. friend would not mind if I anticipated one or two points he made. He has, I am sure, read the very long statement and the schedules and charts which I put on the record on June 14, which bear directly on his topic.
67509-472J
Supply-Labour
Added to that, this year, 1956, is hearing not only many speeches on the part of the principal of McGill University, but by a great many other people. In addition to that, some intensive study is going on on this very topic. This week the second meeting of university representatives and others conferred with us in the Department of Labour and held meetings upon it. Another one is taking place down in my own province of New Brunswick at St. Andrews-by-the-sea early in September on this topic and I assure him, Mr. Chairman, that I do not believe the matter is being overlooked in so far as Canada is concerned.

I am delighted to hear the remarks of the Minister of Labour to the effect that this matter is being carefully considered. As I have already said on previous occasions, this matter has been brought up. It is giving great concern not only to members of this house but to responsible people all over the country.
The other matter I wish to raise at this point is a matter which no doubt has been considered, but I think it should be emphasized again. I believe, in the remarks attributed to Dr. James this morning over the air, the difficulty in Canada was with respect to training technical personnel, engineers and scientists. The difficulty is the fact that there are simply no facilities, or inadequate facilities, at the present time to train the people who might be required. Because of the great difficulty that the municipalities and provincial governments have in financing this matter I know that many universities rely on private donations, which is a very fine thing; but in this country I cannot think of any university that can rely entirely on private donations. They cannot possibly provide the facilities without very substantial help from the provincial governments.
We are faced at the present time-and I think the problem is recognized-with a shortage of technical people and scientists. If this matter is not corrected very soon it may be a matter of life and death to all of us in the near future. The municipal and provincial governments cannot handle it; they have not the finances to do it. The minister has indicated that the Department of Labour is apparently taking an interest in this matter, and is looking into it to see what can be done, or should be done. Undoubtedly, Mr. Chairman, it is a question that is going to land eventually squarely on the shoulders of the federal government. Unless the provinces and the municipalities have more money to construct training facilities for these people they are not going to be able to do it and

Supply-Labour
the federal government is going to have to do it either directly or indirectly. If something is not done about it soon all of us here are going to suffer very severely, and our successors will be more likely to suffer in the future.

Mr. Chairman, since the day on which the minister made his statement to the house there has been a veritable rash of announcements with reference to conferences and studies which are being made. The minister himself just referred to one that is taking place in St. Andrews from September 9 to September 11, sponsored by the dominion council of professional engineers. The conference that the hon. member for Oxford has just spoken about, of course, was announced on the radio this morning. In addition, statements have been made by responsible people on this subject.
In the committee on estimates I think the thing that bothered everyone was the inability to procure information, which we thought that branch of the department would have at its fingertips. When the minister spoke on the introduction of his estimates he produced a very important statement on this matter. At that time it was quite apparent that the information that had not been available in the study of the estimates had been produced in the interim, probably on instructions from the minister's office. If all of these conferences that have taken place and are taking place, and those persons who have seen fit to make statements on this very important matter, could be brought together and their resources and information pooled, probably we would then have the information we seek.
I ask the minister whether the green light has been given to this branch of his department to go ahead, because I am convinced the reason we did not have the information in the first place was that they did not have the authority to proceed with the compilation of the information. Certainly, it did not take very long to get once the matter had been threshed out in the committee. I suggest that the minister should give the green light to the economics and research division of his department to go ahead and procure this information, to pool the resources of those various bodies to see whether we cannot come up with the answer to an extremely important question. This should be done not only at the engineering and scientific level, but also at the technical and vocational level.

Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend's remarks deserve a comment because of the fact that I admitted at once at the first meeting of the estimates committee that

we were armed completely with those things affecting technical training which come within our jurisdiction in relation to the provinces.
As my hon. friend knows, this field divides itself very clearly into two parts. There are the professional, technical personnel and there are the non-professional. We have had the responsibility defined by this parliament to assist in the training of the non-professional technical personnel through the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which we have attempted to develop very fully and very successfully, I think.
In the other field we have approached it, I am frank to say, in part. Under the unemployment insurance commission we have the executive and professional branch, which undertakes not only to compile figures, but to give very active service to executive professional people in finding suitable employment, and to corporations and governments in finding executive and professional people for those services.
The hon. member was kind enough to admit that after a lapse of a few weeks we did procure a fairly creditable survey of the whole field, as is indicated in Hansard of June 14. Since that time we have followed that up. My colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, has under his jurisdiction a great amount of material in the dominion bureau of statistics. We do not feel that it requires parliamentary sanction. Perhaps it does not require that the Department of Labour be especially earmarked for that purpose, but since it is related to manpower, and to the suitable employment of our manpower in Canada, we have this year strengthened our resources for dealing with it.
One other point was made that I should like to mention. It was made in the committee on estimates. The fear was expressed that we were losing a great many of our engineers, and of our professional and scientific people during those years. We are losing some, but we are not losing anything like the number that is sometimes said.
How many?

I have figures for the last three years. This comes from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and covers the influx of engineers from the United States into Canada and the average for those three years coming in from the United States is 140 per year. We have figures concerning those who are going out to the United States and the average is 249 per year so that the net loss is the difference between those two figures.
About 100 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is the minister able to tell us what the influx of engineers has been from England and Europe?
We have not yet been able to get anything like an accurate statement on that but I am glad my colleague has mentioned it because the net is certainly in our favour rather than against us.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I understand that the balance of exports and imports of engineers was about 1,000 in favour of Canada in the year 1955.

Can the minister say whether that is a continuing figure? This is information we found it difficult to procure and no one seems to have this information. I am sure the minister has a personal interest in the matter. Can he tell us if that is a continuing figure or whether it was a sudden spurt in the one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I could not vouch for the figures but it is my understanding that in the post second world war years we have been a net gainer of engineers through immigration.
On page 5067 of Hansard of June 15 there is some information along that line.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the minister that these estimates had a pretty good working over in committee and that several of us did make a general statement previously on these estimates before the minister went overseas, so we in this group have no intention of debating all the details or repeating what has been said.
With respect to the question now before the committee, however, I would just like to say that after discussing it in many places and listening to all the information that was available on the subject I believe the question that has been posed is misleading in that we have been pinpointing a shortage of engineers when actually the question the universities and the country must face is the lack of facilities at universities and the need for capital expansion. There is a shortage of all professional personnel; this is true of the medical profession and the dental profession, and there is a shortage of trained personnel for hospitals in general.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is not so much the case in medicine but there is a real shortage of dentists.

What I am endeavouring to emphasize is the inability of our present university set-up to accommodate students for training in all the professions. If you make a canvass of the universities as to the number of applications that have come
Supply-Labour
in this year from students seeking admission into engineering, medicine, dentistry and the other professions you will find that a great many have been denied admission due to lack of facilities.
I think the crux of the problem is not the shortage of personnel in any one particular group but rather it is the shortage of the capital necessary for universities to expand their facilities; that is the question. It is all right for Professor Cyril James and Mr. Duncan and others to take the Soviet union as a yardstick and to say they are doing so much better than we are in Canada or the United States but this again refers back to the question of the money that is available for the purpose of promoting education in the country. What they should remember is that the Soviet union has all the income that is derived from the whole economy to use as they see fit and to pin point any particular project they feel is in the best interests of the Soviet union. In this country our industries retain their profits but in the Soviet union these profits are used by the government without any restriction and they expend them wherever they feel an emphasis is desirable.
I was glad to note that in the last week at least one industry in Canada indicated that it has become conscious of the real problem in education. International Nickel, for example, a few days ago advertised through the press that they were contributing some $2J million. They use that money, of course, to promote the universities to the best advantage. If we are going to find the money that will answer the problem we are facing in so far as the universities are concerned I believe that more of the industries in this country that see the problem as it actually exists- that is, we are not training sufficient professional personnel because the universities in Canada have not adequate facilities to turn out such qualified graduates-will be led to take such steps. The universities have to find the money to provide facilities to accommodate the student population which is desirous of taking training in the professions. I think we are missing the boat and confusing the issue by merely stating there is a shortage in any one particular professional group.
You can take a look at the manpower situation generally and you will find right across the country that in the national employment offices which come under the jurisdiction of the minister there is a long list of requests for mechanics, bricklayers, carpenters and other skilled tradesmen. We can turn out as many professional people as we like including engineers, but unless there is someone to do the actual job of work that is necessary all our professional training goes by the board

Supply-Labour
because the real producers of wealth and the builders of the nation along with the architects and draftsmen are the mechanics, bricklayers, carpenters and skilled tradesmen who take the diagram from the drawing board and translate it into something tangible.
The problem of education is not an isolated question relating to any one particular professional group. I believe we have to find the money to expand our university facilities. I think the minister and the provincial government have to step up their trade training program in the different provinces across the country in order to get the skilled personnel who are constantly being advertised for in the national employment offices.
I believe what the government is going to have to do is to sit down with all those who are interested and concerned and pin point the question as it actually is which involves getting enough capital to enable our universities to expand their facilities in order to take care of people who require training and in addition to expand trade training facilities across the country to fill the need for the skilled tradesmen who are required at the present time.

I am glad, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to the steps taken by one of our great corporations in this field. I would like to remind the hon. member that the federal government is now doing quite a lot in assisting universities.
I know that.

The federal grant is assisting in a very important fashion. The other day a friend of mine who is the head of one of the great universities of this country sent me his catalogue and attached to that was a thick book listing the scholarships that were available for that university. I took my pencil and ticked off those scholarships, bursaries and other forms of assistance that came from the federal government and they totalled $208,000 for that one year.
It is true, as hon. members who have spoken have indicated, that this professional field is one that needs and is, I think, receiving a great deal of co-ordination and study. The hon. member for Hamilton West mentioned other things that were happening. My deputy minister has reminded me that since we have discussed this there have been discussions going on under the auspices of the manpower committee of the Canadian Manufacturers Association.
We are planning another meeting with the representatives of the engineering, scientific and professional organizations and employers' organizations this fall under the Minister of Labour.
I think we should try to have a very clear understanding of what is happening over the top of the north pole and our task is to estimate how many professional engineers we need here in Canada for our own specific work and then do everything we can toward that end. There have been estimates made as to the requirements of professional manpower and it is the consensus of people who know most about it that our requirements for engineers are now about 3,000 per year. The graduates this year, that is last spring, numbered 1,700, but enrolments have been increasing over the past few years, so much so that the class of 1959 will probably graduate about 2,850. That will be getting close to closing the gap. One might hope that with further activities in the way of immigration of professional people and from other sources we may be able to bridge it reasonably quickly.

Mr. Chairman, the minister made a sound statement when he said that first of all we must know what the problem is. This is a many-faceted problem and the picture is constantly changing. Before you can solve any problem you must know precisely what it is you are tackling. That is why under this particular item dealing with economic research we have to consider this question. As the minister has said, there is also the executive and professional division of the unemployment insurance commission which is studying the problem.
Just to show how quickly the picture can change, in the current report of the director of the executive and professional division of the unemployment insurance commission it is said that three years ago it was thought that Canadian employers would be looking for at least 2,000 graduates. It will be seen that in three years' time that demand will have increased 50 per cent, and by 1959, when the minister says that we will be graduating possibly 2,900, provided there are no dropouts, and there always are, we will still be falling far short of the mark.
I do not want to labour this point, but all those who have to do with this have shown concern. Obviously the first thing to do is to find out what the problem is and to get the best advice we can on how to meet it. I am not overlooking the need for technicians as well, which is most important. People like the Canadian Manufacturers Association and the professional and engineering societies can tell us what the relative need for technicians will be to assist those working in the professional field. It is my opinion that the first thing we should do is to make some projection into the future to find out what we will have to do.

Mr. Chairman, 1 am glad the minister is specially interested in this matter because as a former university president I am sure he is quite aware of the problem. When the estimates of the Department of National Defence were before the committee I asked some questions which the minister told me would be more appropriately answered by the Minister of Labour. I should like to refer to two pamphlets, which I am sure all members of parliament have received, by the general manager of the Chemical Institute of Canada. One is entitled "Science and Mathematics Teaching in our Secondary Schools" and the other "Education of Professional Manpower in the U.S.S.R." In discussing the Canadian problem Dr. Garnet T. Page points out:
Canada faces an unprecedented demand for engineers and scientists, and the demand is likely to continue. This need has created a whole series of problems in education, ranging from the primary and secondary school level, through university undergraduate training to the post-graduate level. All of these problems are of concern to our professional technical societies, and the Chemical Institute of Canada has been studying some of them.
One of these problems-that of what immediate action should be taken to up-grade the level of the teaching of mathematics and science in our secondary schools-is surveyed generally in this article, and a series of suggested measures to ease this problem are put forward, with the objective of having competent and inspiring teachers of mathematics and science in our secondary schools.
Dr. Page then lists a number of constructive suggestions upon which I hope the minister will have some opportunity to comment. In dealing with the education of professional manpower in the U.S.S.R. he gives comparative statistics as between Canada and a number of other countries and points out that the increase in the number of students and teachers in the universities of the U.S.S.R. is a matter of great concern. Mr. J. S. Duncan, president of the Massey-Harris-Ferguson company, has indicated the tremendous interest there is in education in the U.S.S.R. Hon. members who heard him will recall that he visited one plant where 40,000 people were employed and he found that one-quarter of that force or 10,000 persons came back three nights a week from 6.30 until 9.30, some to take up elementary work, some secondary work and some university work. Here we have 10,000 out of 40,000 coming back after a hard day's work, and Mr. Duncan emphasized that it was hard work, because they felt the urge to improve their qualifications.
When the national defence estimates were before us I asked for a report on the conference which had been held some time earlier in the session when various departments of government had looked at this
Supply-Labour
problem. We were able to draw from the Minister of National Defence the information that cadets are trained at a cost of $32,000 each. It seems to me that that presents a problem to Canadians. If we are able to find $32,000 to provide training for a cadet to qualify himself to enter the army, air force or navy, then the Minister of Labour must be prepared to give consideration to the problems which exist in the field of education in order to make it possible for Canada to meet the continuing challenge which is presented to us, particularly by the need of an ample supply of engineers and teachers of mathematics and sciences in our schools, so that we can train a sufficient number of these people.
Can the minister give some report on the question which I posed when the defence estimates were up and when his colleague intimated that he might have something to say later on?

The documents which my hon. friend has in his hands were on the agenda of the discussions which took place this summer and which will continue. My hon. friend referred to the great growth of scientific training in Russia, and spoke of those there who apparently had felt the urge to improve their qualifications. I am inclined to be a little suspicious of that; I am inclined to think that somebody outside felt the urge that they should improve their qualifications and probably used stronger incentives than we would want to use in Canada or that are available in the federal or provincial fields. I have come to the conclusion this year from observing the wholesome interest in Canada not only on the part of the universities but outside that what is needed here is the creating of an atmosphere in which private industry and the universities together with governments, but governments particularly, will take a leading part in carrying out studies and devising plans that should be put into effect to obtain the results that we all want to see as far as Canada is concerned. I can assure my hon. friend that within the limits of my department nothing will be left undone to carry that out.

I do not wish to extend the argument. Dr. Page certainly does not give the impression that people are being forced to take education. If facilities are available so that those who want to improve their educational standards can take advantage of them I think that there are a great many Canadians who would be prepared to continue their education, even after they leave high school. Mr. Duncan gave the impression that the people who have a better education in Russia are the people who have better

Supply-Labour
clothing, better living facilities and a chance to enjoy higher standards of living. He emphasized that their standard of living is low compared with ours, but there is a feeling that if a citizen can get a better education he can expect to have a higher standard of living.
There are many Canadians who would like to have a higher standard of living and who would be prepared to improve their qualifications if they could feel that at the end of one year's study, two years' study or three years' study they would be able to have a better house, a better car, a higher standard of living. I think the minister must get his other colleagues in the government persuaded that Canada can do something better than we are doing in this general field.

On this very matter I wonder whether the minister would tell us if he knows whether there is any cost attached to the post-graduate work that these young people do in Russia. Are the night classes free to them? Does the minister happen to have information on that point?
No, I have not. My inference is that it is a part, as so many things are, of the great state plan to forward the interests of the country under the direction of the state.

The contrast between the situation of these Russian boys and girls and the situation confronting our boys and girls is a matter for very serious thought. If I want to send my boy to university just think of the amount of money I have to find to provide him with board and room and the other things he has to have and the amount of money I have to pay to get him into the university, the amount to keep him there, all the fees and so on. Look at the hurdles our boys and girls have to leap in order to get even an elementary education. I would imagine a good deal of thought should be given to that aspect of the question in our general search for a solution.

Item agreed to.
184. Administration of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, $10,500.

While this is not strictly pertinent to item 184, I should like to ask the minister this question. Now that the equal pay legislation has passed the house and will become effective shortly, I presume, what division of the department will administer it? Will it be put under the fair employment practices division, under the women's division or where will it be administered?
It will come in a general way under the industrial relations branch but the women's bureau will have certain duties with respect to it under that branch.
That will be under vote 182.
Under both.

Item agreed to.
185. International labour conferences, $67,720.
I wonder whether my hon. friend will allow me to reply to that question first?
Certainly.

It is quite a hard one and I do not want to be confronted with another one before answering it.
I know that my hon. friend is devoted to democratic practices not only in his political life but in his attitude toward labour particularly. It is not what the minister thinks in these matters that governs; it is what the organizations think; I refer to the organizations which provide their representatives for these special purposes. When we go to them and ask them if they will please nominate what they consider is their most representative delegate for this particular purpose, I do not think it is for me, as Minister of Labour, to question Mr. "X" when they give that name as a nominee or for me to question the Seafarers International Union when I make the same request of them. That is exactly what happened in these cases. The Canadian Labour Congress was asked and the Canadian Labour Congress in turn asked the Seafarers International Union. I have no doubt whatever that the Canadian Manufacturers Association, on the one hand, and the Canadian Labour Congress and their affiliated organization, namely the Seafarers International Union, on the other, felt that these two gentlemen filled the purpose that was needed at this special conference.

Might I say just a word on that point, Mr. Chairman. When the minister's department solicit nominations, as I presume they do, from these bodies, how simple it would be for the department to ask for Canadian citizens. We assume they will be Canadian citizens. We just naturally assume that. I do not think that the Canadian Manufacturers Association on the one hand or the Canadian Labour Congress on the other

Supply-Labour
ever thought about the fact that they were nominating persons who were not Canadian citizens. As the hon. member for Kootenay West has said, there is a difference in the two nominees. But nevertheless, even if they nominate citizens in ignorance of the rules of the ILO and if they nominate individuals who are not citizens of Canada, it would seem to me that it is the duty of the minister's department-and this particular division has a director paid by his department-to say to these organizations: "This individual, who may be a highly respected person and a well-qualified person in so far as he personally is concerned, is not an acceptable nominee to this department by reason of the fact that he is not a Canadian citizen".

While I have not gone as far as my hon. friend has gone, I should like to point out that during the last several years, in writing for nominations from employer and worker organizations we have pointed out and have stressed the desirability of the person nominated to us being a Canadian citizen, and we will continue to do so.

I was extremely glad to hear the minister say that, Mr. Chairman. I think it is most improper that this country should be represented abroad-either employers or employees-by citizens of other countries. I should like to ask the minister this question. Does he bring to the attention of these organizations this rule in the ILO constitution which says that they must be most representative? I think it takes a great stretch of the imagination to say that the citizens of another country are most representative of Canadians when they go to an international labour congress.
That rule is well known to those who nominate their representatives.
Can the minister explain why the Department of Labour paid the expenses directly of the delegate of the Canadian Manufacturers Association?

Yes. Without going into the details of the matter, may I say this. There are some of the activities of the ILO in connection with which the ILO budget takes care of the expenses. Mind you, we contribute to the ILO budget to quite an extent. We assist to that degree. There are also other meetings in connection with which the Department of Labour is called upon to pay the expenses of the delegates, I refer not only to departmental delegates or government delegates but other delegates as well. It just happens that way. There is nothing invidious about it.

Just in conclusion I want to say this. I trust that in future the employers organizations in this country and the trade unions will have sufficient pride in being Canadians to nominate Canadians to represent us at the ILO.
Thank you very much.

The matter on which I should like to ask the minister a question does not come under this item. I wonder whether he can tell me under what item I might ask it. We are given to understand that there is a heavy advance in the price of steel. I want to ask the minister whether there is any means whereby he consults -with people like the steel companies in respect of any proposed advance in price in order to make sure that that advance in price is completely justified. Under what item could I ask concerning that matter?
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that matter does not come under any item that I can think of in my estimates.
Could the minister suggest under whose department it would come?

I would hate to suggest it, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps, as we go along, my hon. friend would give it consideration and we would see where it might fit in. But I am quite sure that I cannot think of any item in my estimates where it would appropriately fit.

Item agreed to.
187. To provide for expenses of the women's bureau, $26,958.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to pause at this item because the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Timiskaming in the corridors and the hon. member for Hamilton West in the house have put forward the point of view that there should not be any delay in the promulgation of the bill which is now awaiting royal assent. I think this would be the most appropriate place to make a statement on the matter. I can state that as soon as royal assent is given-which I hope will be before too many days-
I certainly do.

-my officials will forward to our fair wage officers and to the larger employers of women coming under federal jurisdiction a copy of the act so that they may have it and be able to study it. I shall also recommend to the governor in council that the act be promulgated on October 1, 1956.
Item agreed to.
189. To provide for expenditures incurred in connection with manpower utilization, labour-management relations and related programs as may be authorized by the Minister of Labour, $30,000.

I had prepared a couple of 30 minute speeches on this item, but I am going to throw my notes to the winds and take about two minutes. This is not a very large item, only $30,000, but it involves, I believe, a very important principle and that is what can be done by the minister's department to help settle differences between labour and management. The question raised a moment ago by the hon. member for Lethbridge is a little bit pertinent to this item and I think it could have been discussed under this item, but I shall leave it with him to determine whether he thinks it should be.
The point is this. In my opinion labour and management can never get together to solve what we believe to be a flaw in the present system whereby, in the over-all picture, prices and wages can never come together. The present monetary policy of the government, based on a flaw, will never provide enough purchasing power within industry to buy back the products of industry. The result is that every time there is an increase in wages, then that must be written into costs and by reason of the rise in the price level the people suffer because that generates a shortage of purchasing power. All I would say is that it is a problem of automation; that is what labour calls it now. It does seem to me that the trend is to try to guarantee something within industry which cannot be guaranteed because it is not there. If industry does not generate enough purchasing power to buy back its products, then that flaw must be corrected.
In our social credit concept-I am not going into the details of economics on it-we have that problem solved by what we determine is the compensated price or what might be in the end a national dividend to make up that shortage of purchasing power.
Carried.
No, my friend, it is not carried, but I am not going to detain the house.
What item are you on?

On 189; I am advocating this, that the Minister of Labour, who has a responsibility in this connection together with the Minister of Finance who also has a responsibility in this connection, solve that flaw in a way whereby the economic system will work so that there will be enough purchasing power by reason of wages plus dividends or wages plus a compensated discount on price, to keep the system functioning 67509-473i
Supply-Labour
so that the Canadian people can always buy back the results of the production of industry.
I have said a lot there. If it is not going to be solved that way, then the trend is to push all industry into the hands of government and what the socialists have been advocating, government ownership of industry, will be accomplished but not by the socialists but by a flaw that is presently and always has been in the financial policy of the government. Labour and management will do that themselves unconsciously, but that is exactly what will happen if that problem is not solved. I have compacted a 30 minute speech into a few sentences.

It may be in order here to ask this question in another form. I asked about the steel problem. We in the west, and in Alberta, are being absolutely crucified by freight rates. They seem to have the idea we can bear the full shot to remedy freight rates all over the country. They will not be satisfied until they are walking over our dead bodies. If the railway men ask for higher wages and the C.P.R. or the C.N.R. just increase their rates enough to cover that increase in wages, that is one thing. But if they say, very well, it is going to cost us $30 million more to pay the wages and we are going to take a little rake-off out of this thing, we are going to take $35 million; if that kind of think is done, and I am afraid it is, not only in the case of the railways but in the case of most industries in Canada, then it is obviously a most iniquitous situation. As the hon. member for Macleod has indicated, if it is not taken care of it will mean the utter destruction of our economy and our free way of life.
I just wonder if the minister has any department under which he does investigate to make sure that if a company has to pay an additional amount for wages, it takes out of its consumers just enough to cover that additional amount and not that additional amount plus a substantial rake-off. Has the minister any department that looks into that matter? It seems to me he should have the knowledge anyway; he should have the information.

When the hon. member for
Macleod was speaking I did not interrupt, Mr. Chairman, because I felt that there were some things he was saying very forcibly that were related to these estimates. However, I am quite sure the hon. member for Lethbridge has given unto the Minister of Labour powers that he could not gain. The minister's main preoccupation in the field the hon. member has mentioned comes under item 182. I am free to admit that there the primary consideration is to maintain industrial

Supply-Labour
peace as between management and labour in those industries that come under the federal jurisdiction. It would probably be very good if the Minister of Labour could investigate all those factors scientifically and work out a formula that would achieve stability within our economy such as outlined by the hon. member for Lethbridge. But I would be untrue if I were to say he could do it under our present set-up. It would be true to say that I will co-operate with my colleagues in every way I possibly can in achieving some of the results that the hon. member would like to see.

I should like to make one more comment. I am not suggesting the Minister of Labour necessarily has the power to bring about the adjustment I am suggesting. I am suggesting that the knowledge should be accumulated in his department so he will be able to tell whether there is any form of extravagant increase blamed upon increases in wages. Has he any department through which he gains the knowledge?
We acquire information, and that is one of the roles of our research branch.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

minister was going to call it one o'clock be-for he passed the last two items. I am willing to let it ride on 190.
