AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.
Vocational training co-ordination-
194. To provide for carrying out the purposes of the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act and agreements made thereunder; to authorize the Minister of Labour to enter into agreements with any province on terms approved by the governor in council to provide financial assistance to vocational schools, and training under youth training projects and to provide for the expenditures thereunder and under vocational training agreements entered into in previous years-payments to the provinces, $4,515,150.

Mr. Chairman, I have looked over the report of the department and I have also read the minutes of the estimates committee and I find it difficult to reconcile the various amounts set out in various ways for vocational training. I wonder if the minister would simply break down the total of $4,515,150 for the provinces?
Does my hon. friend wish me to break it down in addition to the breakdown on page 259?

As I see it the
breakdown on page 259 relates to the various types of training and in the report it is broken down in the same way but on a somewhat more detailed basis. I wonder if the minister would break down the total for each of the ten provinces for all purposes covered by the section?
Mr. Chairman, at the very bottom of page 259 payments to the provinces are indicated for 1955-56 and for the coming year 1956-57 and the latter is shown in the left-hand column.
I am asking the minister to advise us how much was paid to Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and to each of the other provinces, breaking down the total amount.
May I give it in round figures?
That would be quite satisfactory.

For the fiscal year 1955-56 for Newfoundland it was $835,000. I am sorry; the figure I have just given you is the total accumulated figure since the inception of the vocational plan but I think what my hon. friend wants is the breakdown for one year.
Payments to April 30, 1956 for fiscal year 1955-56 are as follows:	Newfoundland,
$135,000; Prince Edward Island, $34,000; Nova Scotia, $373,000; New Brunswick, $233,000; Quebec, $647,000; Ontario, $1,073,000; Manitoba, $352,000; Saskatchewan, $307,000; Alberta, $491,000; British Columbia, $309,000; Northwest Territories, $6,000; Yukon, $2,000.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the
minister will not mind repeating the sums for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
Does my hon. friend wish me to repeat the figures I gave a moment ago?
Yes.
For Quebec it was $647,000 and for Ontario $1,073,000.
Do those figures include the two items which are listed on page 83 of the department's report under tables 7 and 8 for the training of armed forces and defence industries?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, can the minister explain the reason for the difference-of course, I am not jealous-between the figures for the province of Quebec and the province

of Ontario? Is it a lack of co-operation on the part of Quebec or is it for some other reason that the amount for Quebec is so much lower than the amount for Ontario?

My hon. friend will see that in the figures I have given there is no particular relationship at all with the population of the ten provinces. There are a number of schedules of training; some provinces want to put stress on one and some on another. We co-operate with the provinces in doing what they think will serve the best purpose.
Does that ippan the province of Ontario has done more lit that sphere of activity than has the province of Quebec?
That effort is indicated by the figures I have given.
I am just asking these questions of the minister because we were told something different at the last provincial election.
Where do you think that will get you?

Item agreed to.
Unemployment insurance commission-
196. Administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act. including expenditures incurred in connection with other duties and responsibilities assumed and carried out as required by the governor in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour in accordance with section 4 of the act, $27,341,745.

Mr. Chairman, concerning this item, which covers the administration of unemployment insurance, we in this group feel that we have had a very satisfactory survey of the department. When I say that,
I do not mean we are satisfied with everything that has happened but we feel we have had ample opportunity, both in the committee and during the stages of the recent resolution and bill with respect to amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, to ask questions and obtain the information we wanted.
I have only one more comment to make and although I have said it three times before I feel I must say it again. In the application of recent amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act with regard to section 45 (2) I urge the minister from the start to keep a very close watch on the application of these amendments in order to make sure we do not get into any kind of difficulty during this coming period of seasonal unemployment as we did last year.
The revised act is still new. We have gone through one season when we did not measure up to the expectations of that act. Although we may think we have improved
Supply-Labour
the act, for those will apply in the future, I feel very strongly that the portion of the
100,000	people, if that is the figure, who failed to qualify last year because of changed conditions from the old act to the new act, or other persons taking their places, should not again face the same problem nor should they be placed in a similar position.
There may be a tendency to think we have cured the situation and it may well be that it has been cured; but the people who suffered a serious period of unemployment even for one season without proper compensation-and they might well be excused if they thought they deserved compensation
do not re-establish themselves quickly. Such people pile up debts and go through a period of dislocation which is disastrous to them.
The people who were cut off from receiving benefits last year-whatever the number might have been-are going to suffer as the result of this cut-off for a long period of time. I hope the minister will start early to keep a watchful eye on this situation and instruct his officials to consider this matter seriously and that they will endeavour to the best of their ability to avoid a recurrence of the situation which developed last year.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend gives me the opportunity to say what I think should be said in relation to the first part of her remarks. It has been said in this chamber at other times that the estimates committee was to some extent useless and did not perform its purpose. I want to testify this afternoon that in so far as my estimates are concerned I value most highly the study and criticism and suggestions which were made in the estimates committee when we were before it.
On the other point, may I say that the new act came into effect on October 2 last year. This is August 11, not yet a year after, and yet we have tried to insert this session what was conceived by all of us to be something that should have been in the old act. I can tell my hon. friends of the committee that we will continue to watch it with the utmost vigilance.

Obviously the difficulty arose when the regulations were put Into effect. We foresaw this potentiality when we studied it last year. None of us in committee had had any control over the regulations or the interpretation of the regulations or of the act. We had no control over that at all, we could only view it as we saw it. Then these things come along at the administrative level.
If I had a criticism to make it would be that I believe that the minister and his

Supply-Labour
department are swayed by the findings of the actuaries. In my estimation the role of an actuary is to tell the department how much they will need to perform a given service, not to say to them, "You cannot do this because you have not enough money." I think the minister should make sure that the viewpoint of his department is what is required and how much do we need, not how much do we have and how much can we do. Let us proceed on that basis. The role of the actuary is extremely important, but he is not a policy making authority. So let us not get off on that track.

Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of grievances I want to bring before the minister. If he cannot give me an answer now perhaps he can let me have one some time in the near future. I will not go into these in detail but it seems to be the whole crux of the thing that one woman who is complaining is the wife of a man working in the air force. He was moved to Gimli in my constituency and apparently her crime was that she followed her man. She left her job in Montreal or St. John, Quebec, and followed her husband to Gimli and reported for work there. She cannot get any benefits according to the data I have here.
I think that is a most unreasonable stand to take simply because she gave up a job
2,000	miles away and followed her husband and tried to get work somewhere else. She has been paying into the insurance fund for a long time. Then I see here a rather hard blow to the town of Gimli because they say it is a small civilian settlement. I hope the people in Gimli never know that that is on the record. That is one of the oldest settled districts in the interlake country because the Icelanders settled there in 1871. There are approximately 3,000 people at the air base and the town is growing by leaps and bounds. There is a lot of work there. I do not want to be as bad as other people by talking too long.
The only crime this other woman committed was to stop work when she was going to have a baby. When she had her baby she applied for work and they said, "Go to Winnipeg." Winnipeg is 65 miles away so it would be a round trip of 130 miles. You cannot expect anyone to travel 130 miles a day unless he is well enough off to have a plane.
I do not think either of these women has committed a crime but they have both been denied any relief or recognition by the unemployment insurance commission.

First of all I want to apologize to the residents of Gimli because of the comment indicating that it is not a very large

place. I do not think the cases mentioned by the hon. member have been submitted to me. I shall not have much to do for the next few days and if my hon. friend will send them to me with such explanatory information as he may have I shall have them both carefully reviewed.
Thank you very much; I shall be pleased to do that.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two observations at this time. I did not participate in the debate to amend the Uneidpfoyment Insurance Act but I want to assure the minister that we appreciate the amendments which were brought in and are sure they will be of real value to the various groups of people concerned.
I believe the purpose of the unemployment insurance commission is to facilitate the granting of benefits to those who qualify and in order to do that I would imagine that to have offices in strategic places would be of great importance. A short time ago I brought to the attention of the officials of the department the situation existing in Hope, British Columbia, in my own riding. The people there have requested that an office be opened but apparently up to the present the officials have not seen fit to recommend this. This afternoon I should like to request the minister to look into this situation. I feel an office in Hope is justified because this is a vital section and there would be a considerable amount of work. I ask the minister to re-examine the situation.
Just one other thing. During the period when the C.P.R. bridge was not available, having collapsed, the unemployment insurance office at Mission was moved to Abbotsford on a temporary basis. However, we feel that the continuation of this office on a permanent basis is warranted after the bridge has been repaired. On request of my constituents I ask that this office be continued on a permanent basis for the benefit of the people there.

Mr. Chairman, I shall ask the commission to look into the two cases mentioned. I think I must point out to the hon. member that there are many hon. members on all sides of the house who would like to have offices opened up at additional points in their ridings, but I am sure the hon. member will understand the importance of economy. We have about 200 offices across Canada and in attempting to serve the needs of the workers in the best possible way we try to carry on from those offices without adding to the amount we must ask for for the administration of this act. I shall ask that these two cases be looked into.

With reference to this section of the Unemployment Insurance Act, as I mentioned on August 6 at the resolution stage of the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act, this section 67 (1) (c) (iv) with reference to married women is pointed up again by the remarks of the member for Selkirk. I have heard all the arguments for years with reference to why there should be special provisions for married women in the act, but it occurs to me that the minister and his officials are quite willing to gamble in the application of the act to other groups of employees. When it comes to this one specific group, they lay down these hard and fast rules which cannot be altered. I have approached the minister previously on other grounds. I now ask him if he will not gamble a little and remove this provision from the act, that is, remove section 67 (1) (c) (iv) and section 161 of the regulations, and see what happens.

I am sure that my hon. friend would not want me to start gambolling at my age, but we shall continue to look at this question of married women with the utmost care as we have in the past. I am sure that in the past year we have improved the regulations to some extent.
I should not like to ask the minister to do anything that he had not done up to this time of his life, but in regard to the Unemployment Insurance Act there was a big gamble in the act last year.
As it affects married women?
As it affects the 100,000 workers.

Whilst the married women section is part of the act, there is another question he raised-and it is not a new one-on the matter of administration. I think that this centre here is affected to a greater extent than any other part of Canada. At least to me, the problem seems to be mainly around Ottawa. There are many army, navy and air force personnel around this city, and in many cases both the husband and wife are working. The man in the service suddenly gets an order that he is being transferred to Vancouver, Halifax or some other point.
In order to maintain the home, naturally the woman wants to follow her husband, and so she goes to Halifax. The reason why she leaves her employment is that an order has been issued by the service authorities. To maintain her home she has to go with her husband and leave her employment. When she arrives in Halifax she cannot find similar work. Perhaps she has been contributing for ten years to the unemployment insurance.
Supply-Labour
It is through no fault of her own that she has to go to another part of the country. There is nothing in the act that says that that woman cannot draw unemployment insurance in Halifax. I think it is a matter for the minister and the commission to determine the validity of permitting that woman to draw benefits under the circumstances I have just described.
That is one matter that the member for Selkirk raised. The other one, of course, has been beaten to death. As I said at the resolution stage, there has been considerable modification of the application of the regulations to married women.
It should not be there.
I have said that myself but I know now it is useless to repeat it. The minister, since last March, has been making efforts.
He has been trying. He won't give up.
He might start gambling.

There are more cases than we get in this house. It is a matter for the commission to determine whether that woman is entitled to unemployment insurance benefits when she has to follow her husband to another part of the country. That is a matter of administration. There is nothing in the act to stop it. I believe the minister and the commission should take a good, square look at that. Quite a few people that were located in Ottawa had to go to Halifax. A woman cannot find the kind of employment there that she can here. It is not fair.

There can be no question that the more you look into the unemployment insurance commission the more you come to the conclusion that it is one of the worst operated branches of the government. Last winter I brought up the question of some delays to unemployment insurance cases. At first the minister said there were no delays; then he admitted there were six; then he admitted there were 206; then it went up to 7,106 cases. That is the answer I got in March. That is the number of claims referred to the regional office at Moncton by the Campbellton and Edmundston offices. In each and every one of those cases there was an unwarranted delay, in some cases up to eight weeks, to determine the rights of the people to draw unemployment insurance benefits.
I maintain that there is no reason in this world why it should take so long to determine a man's rights to unemployment insurance benefits. I make this recommendation

Supply-Labour
to the minister, that he take the means now, this summer and this fall, to make sure that next winter we shall not have a repetition of the debacle that happened in northern New Brunswick last winter with regard to the collection of unemployment insurance benefits. These people have families and they cannot get along without those benefits. Real hardship, of which the minister may not be aware, is inflicted on those families just because they have not taken the means to handle those cases expeditiously and quickly.
Another thing I should like to bring up is this. What is this idea of forcing people, especially people on the north shore of New Brunswick, to go 400 or 500 miles away from home? Last winter there was an order to send 300 or 400 to La Tuque, Quebec, to cut pulpwood. These people were made to work under such conditions in the woods outside La Tuque that they were not able to earn enough money to pay their fare back home, and it took months afterwards to get their unemployment insurance cases straightened out. There was no reason to give that order in the first place. I recommend that, before any such stupid order is given, an investigation should be made to determine the working conditions and the chances of earning a living in the place where they wish the men to go.
Some of the men were able to get by these stupid regulations in the Unemployment Insurance Act by saying that their wives were sick and they had to return home. Many had to lie, because not all of them had their wives sick, to get out of the obligation to go to La Tuque, where they could not earn enough money to get back home, and if they did not get their unemployment insurance benefits they would be cut off indefinitely.
The minister will say that he has fine employees in the unemployment insurance offices in New Brunswick, and he is absolutely correct. The fault is not theirs; the fault is with him here in Ottawa. Let us get that straight. In Campbellton, Edmundston and Moncton, the people in the unemployment insurance offices do everything within their power to accommodate the people. Every time I have gone to them, they have gone out of their way to find out the reasons for the difficulties, and then they point to some stupid regulation which forces the men to go to La Tuque, or some silly regulation which prevents the person from getting unemployment insurance benefits at a time when he needs it.
There is another matter I should like to bring up. How are we getting along in the matter of bringing about a reciprocity agreement with the state of Maine? In Madawaska

county, according to the figures given by one of the unemployment offices in northern New Brunswick, 1,800 people have to go to Maine to make a living. While in Maine, they have to pay unemployment insurance in that state.
I understand there are only two states in all the United States that do not have reciprocal agreements with Canada in regard to unemployment insurance. In other words, if a fellow went to work in New York state, he would get unemployment insurance benefits on his return to New Brunswick or to Canada. But in the state of Maine, as I am informed by the officials of the unemployment insurance commission, there is no such reciprocity agreement. I maintain that if there is not such an agreement, efforts should be made at the present time to make sure that this reciprocity agreement is entered into before the coming winter in order to make sure that these people-the ones that return home after working in Maine-will be able to collect unemployment insurance benefits. The case does not apply so much to the state of Maine, I will readily admit, because there is more woods work, and there are more activities going on, in northern Maine than there are in northeastern New Brunswick. But 1,800 people are affected, and that is only in my province. It is asserted that over 6,000 people are affected in other localities in Canada along the Maine border.
Another matter to which I would like to direct attention is this. We sometimes ask ourselves why it is that people are leaving the farm. It is bad enough, I think, when you see farmers in the position of being unable to do anything about getting unemployment insurance benefits. But here is the problem. The farmers' helpers, the people who are employed as farm hands, do not get unemployment insurance benefits. For that reason they are reluctant to work on the farms. One farmer after another in my area has come to me and said that if this regulation were changed he might be able to obtain help and to retain it.

I wonder if I might interrupt the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska at this point. The first three points that he mentioned, of which I have taken careful note, are in order under this heading. The present one is not in order because under this item nothing can be done about it.
About which?
If my hon. friend had wanted to debate that matter, he would have been able to debate it on another occasion.
You have done nothing about it.

With regard to the application of unemployment insurance to workers on the farm, may I say that nothing can be done about it under this item which we are discussing at the present time. While I am on my feet-
I am advocating it, and I am suggesting that you do something about it.
Advocate it on the proper occasion.
That is all right. An occasion existed during this session-

I made the suggestion
during this session, on two other occasions.
You were not here.
I brought this matter up on two other occasions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Perhaps my hon. friend would permit me to answer his question. The only one that I think is deserving of an answer of the first three is the one relating to the state of Maine. I can assure him that the commission has consistently and steadily- as it has done with corresponding states right along the United States border across Canada -tried, and is still trying, to work out reciprocity arrangements with the state of Maine with regard to unemployment insurance. We have hopes that this result might be achieved. However, it takes time. I can assure the hon. member or rather I can assure the workers in New Brunswick that it is not the fault of the unemployment insurance commission that there has been delay.

Mr. Chairman, the point I am making is this. I do not think the minister is taking the means to bring it about sufficiently well. He is not doing it properly, I think if it were done properly, this reciprocity agreement could be prepared within a very short time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the last speaker in what he has just said. I agree that he is probably out of order in dealing with casual farm workers, but the minister has not yet told us whether any steps have been taken to protect these people. In my own particular riding I know that fruit workers such as pickers and so on spend part of their time in the packing houses, that they are obliged to contribute their stamps but that they never get any benefits. Year after year we have brought this matter up. It is true, as the minister says, that it is out of order at the moment to discuss the matter but he has not this session given us an answer to our constant
Supply-Finance
requests. That request is: Will these people at some time be taken care of? That is all the previous speaker wanted to know. It is also something that I should like to know because, when I go back to my riding, these people will ask me, "What are they going to do about the casual farm worker in the fruit industry?" It is a serious problem. At the present time, where they are obliged to contribute to the unemployment insurance fund while employed in the packing houses, I think the government is taking the money from them under false pretences because they are not being covered at any time.
Hear, hear. That is very true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there have been several occasions during this session on which I have promised to say something about fiscal and monetary policies. I propose to do so very briefly at the moment.
The fiscal and monetary policies of Canada are intended, among other things, to encourage the sustained growth of our economy within the framework of a stable, over-all price level. With steady economic growth we can support a rapidly-growing population and a steady increase in standards of living. I think it will be agreed that in the years that have passed since the end of the war in Korea this objective of sustained growth, stable prices and higher standards of living has been reasonably well achieved.
We all know, of course, that there are various external and internal forces that may from time to time prevent the stable growth of the economy. For example, Canada cannot enjoy steady growth and high employment if powerful adverse factors restrict or limit the markets for our products at home or abroad. Nor can we maintain stable prices if world price levels are being subjected to great fluctuations, as was the case during the Korean war and, of course, in all other wars. Having said all this, it still remains true that proper monetary and fiscal policies can exert an important stabilizing influence on the economy.
I turn now to consider the special economic circumstances that have had to be taken into account in formulating fiscal and monetary policies so far during 1956. Hon. members will recall that in my budget address four months ago I suggested that 1956 would be

Supply-Finance
another year of substantial economic progress. However, I pointed out that the high level of business activity that was anticipated for 1956 would probably exert considerable pressure on the available supplies of materials, manpower and other economic resources, and that it was, therefore, desirable that the spending policies of everyone should emphasize restraint and prudence. Only in this way would it be possible to avoid inflation or other distortion that might otherwise develop.
As one looks around the country today it is apparent that most of our industries are even busier than was anticipated earlier this year. The statistics confirm this observation, but I need not go into details as they have been discussed by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I should refer, however, to the latest survey suggesting investment outlays of about $8 billion. This level of capital investment, if it is achieved, would be 28 per cent above last year's. This gives one some idea of the momentum which is behind the present expansion of the economy.
I need hardly say that the steady year-by-year increase in the physical plant and equipment of Canada is the thing which more than anything else is making possible the growth in the productivity of our economy. As such it is providing for the steady increase in the welfare of the Canadian people and is therefore something to be welcomed by all of us.
However, this enormous increase in investment planned for 1956 must take place at a time when our export industries are producing more, at a time when the industries which produce goods and services for the consumer are also producing more, and at a time when employment is already at a high level. It is very doubtful therefore whether we have in Canada the plant, the raw materials and the manpower to achieve such a heavy increase in capital investment in full, along with the expected increase in exports, consumer goods and services and all the other things that are needed.
This huge scale of investment in plant and equipment is also reflected in the very high level of imports, and in the large inflow of non-resident money which in effect is financing the import surplus.
I think I have said enough to indicate that in my view there is some danger that, in the months immediately ahead of us, the total rate of spending will tend to run ahead of the ability of the economy to produce more goods and services quickly enough. This means that some additional investment which is being planned today simply will not

be fully realized because of the physical limitations already mentioned.
In these circumstances, what kind of fiscal and monetary policies are appropriate? In the first place I would say that government policies should not contribute unnecessarily to the increased demand for goods and services. With this in mind, and anticipating that 1956 would be a year of heavy private and industrial spending, government expenditures were carefully scrutinized before the estimates were brought down early in 1956. In particular, the capital programs of the various departments were reduced to the essential requirements.
So far as the monetary situation is concerned, the increase in the demand for credit has been the outstanding feature of the last 15 months. Money has been in demand for many purposes but especially to finance new business investment in plant, equipment and inventories, and the increased use of consumer credit. Evidence of this can be found in the tremendous increase of the chartered banks' loans. The total of their general business and personal loans outstanding, after remaining relatively stable through 1954 and the first quarter of 1955 at about $3J billion, has risen continuously since then, and at its present level of $4i billion is 39 per cent higher than it was 16 months ago.
Of course, the availability of funds has also been growing. Larger amounts are being saved out of our larger national income, more funds have been raised through new security issues and more capital has flowed into Canada from abroad. However, the increases in the supply of loanable funds has not kept pace with the increase in the demand for them. Consequently, interest rates have risen.
This growth in the demand for loanable funds is the fundamental explanation of rising interest rates and the increasing tightness of money over the last year or so. That is the real explanation of why it is more difficult and more expensive today for all borrowers to obtain the capital they need. This means, of course, that the tremendous rate of development of our economy calls for the encouragement of the maximum rate of saving in Canada. In this connection I am announcing today the terms of the forthcoming issue of Canada Savings Bonds, which will include an increased return to investors.
Of course it would have been possible for the Bank of Canada to facilitate such an expansion of credit that all these demands for money could have been satisfied without any increase in interest rates. However, if this had been done there would then have been

too much money competing for the available goods, and inflationary price increases would have followed. What the Bank of Canada has been doing has been to moderate the rate of increase in the expansion of credit, so as to keep it in a reasonable relationship with the growth of production. This helps to prevent the present condition of expanding production from spilling over into one of speculation, inflation and instability.
The government is satisfied, and I believe that the vast majority of informed observers are satisfied, that under the economic conditions of the past 12 months it was desirable to moderate the rate of monetary expansion. I know of no responsible person who argues openly for inflation as a solution to the problem of excess demand.
I need hardly say that a condition of "tight money" performs a very important function in our kind of economic system in present circumstances. That is because it compels the borrowers and the lenders of money to review their plans and, if necessary, to revise them. This helps to ensure that the aggregate of all spending plans is consistent with the aggregate production that is physically possible.
The demand for funds for different economic purposes will naturally change from time to time. Similarly, the view of lending institutions as to where they want to invest their resources will also change as economic conditions change. Such changes are necessary and desirable in a changing economy. However, one consequence is that no specific group of borrowers can expect to be provided with a continually growing supply of funds regardless of developments in the other parts of the economy.
Yesterday I was asked about the bank rate. In establishing the level of its bank rate, the Bank of Canada must have regard for the level of interest rates generally as they are determined from day to day in the bond-market. The federal government has a number of separate issues of bonds outstanding in the market and the market price and yield on each issue has some bearing on the appropriate level of bank rate. Attention is often focussed on the yield of treasury bills because this is the shortest term government security outstanding and its yield is well publicized each week through publication of the rate at which the weekly tender issue has been allotted. However, the yield on the 91-day treasury bills is only one factor in the general market pattern of interest rates and the degree of movement in the various government issues is usually by no means uniform. In recent weeks short-term bond yields have risen somewhat more than the yield on treasury bills.
Sup p ly-Finance
Perhaps I can summarize what I have been saying in a few sentences. First, 1956 looks like being the most prosperous year in our history for most of our industries and most of our people. The principal risk that we face- and it is one which we share with a number of other countries-is that the spirit of optimism that exists today may give rise to efforts to spend more on goods and services than the economy is physically capable of producing. If this should happen, distortions in prices and production would result, and the steady expansion of the whole economy might be jeopardized.
The growth in the demand for capital is reflected in higher rates of interest and greater difficulty in borrowing funds of one kind or another. This, of course, is part of the self-correcting process which helps keep our economy on an even keel. It is better to have rising rates of interest, if necessary, than sky-rocketing prices.
It is right and proper that our fiscal system at this juncture should emphasize additional restraint in public spending wherever possible. It is equally appropriate that monetary policy should assist by exerting a moderating influence on the expansion of credit.
With proper fiscal and monetary policies and with reasonable self-disciplines on the part of all of us, there is no reason why our economic progress should not continue in line with the growth in our external markets.

The estimates of the Department of Finance, Mr. Chairman, require a special word of comment at the outset because of their very large bulk. The estimates of this department this year total the tremendous sum of $979,412,104. It is well to remember however, that of this large total $940,369,028 are statutory items, the largest being interest to be paid upon Dominion of Canada bonds. The amount actually to be voted, in other words, the sum that this committee of supply is dealing with this afternoon, is $39,043,076. In that sum there are two substantial items, the grant to universities of $7,986,000 and the grants to municipalities of $7,065,500. The bulk of the remaining estimates is composed of salaries and wages.
Ordinarily a review of the estimates of this department does provide an opportunity for a wide review of such questions as fiscal relations between the federal and provincial jurisdictions, monetary policy, and indeed broad economic questions on which it is sometimes hard to define limits. However, we had in this house quite recently an extensive debate on federal-provincial fiscal relations and I have no intention of entering that field again today. The views of Her

Supply-Finance
Majesty's loyal opposition were completely set forth in the speeches made at the various stages of the measure that was then under
debate.
There is, however, one question in regard to policy which does call at this time for special discussion in this house. The subject itself has become rather broader by reason of some of the remarks that have been made by the Minister of Finance and by the Prime Minister yesterday. The question arose, of course, out of measures that have been taken to restrict credit, and in particular to raise the interest rate of the Bank of Canada. In view of the turn the discussion has taken, particularly in the light of the answers given in this house to questions by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, what we now have brought into question is the relationship between the government on the one hand and the Bank of Canada on the other, and also the relationship between the Bank of Canada on the one hand and this parliament on the other.
Without going back over all the answers that the Minister of Finance has given, both yesterday and on previous occasions about two months ago, I wish to say in all earnestness to the Minister of Finance that his answers have been evasive. I urge on him that, having regard to the responsibilities that he holds and the importance of the subjects to which the questions were directed, questions that affect all the people of this country, and questions that touch the prosperity and well-being of the country, I think his answers ought to have been much more direct.
Now, sir, the Prime Minister answered some questions yesterday in a way that I think startled hon. members of this house. At page 7352 of yesterday's Hansard the Prime Minister said:
The Prime Minister will not undertake to have parliament or the members of the opposition act as a court of appeal from the decision made by the governor of the Bank of Canada-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman complete the answer I gave?

Yes. There was an interjection and then the Prime Minister continued: -unless and until parliament amends the act which now governs the Bank of Canada.
The Prime Minister also indicated there is no intention on the part of the government to introduce any such amendment. Therefore, as things now stand-and that is what we are talking about-the Prime Minister has said that as the law stands today he is not going to have parliament, or members of the opposition, act as a court of appeal from the decision of the governor of the Bank of

Canada. It was superfluous for the Prime Minister to say he was not going to have members of the opposition act in that capacity, because it has been made quite clear during this session that in the view of the Prime Minister the opposition has a very limited function; but I do take up the statement that the Prime Minister made that, in effect, as the law now stands parliament has no right to act as a court of appeal from a decision of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Unless and until the act is changed.

We are saying, as the law now stands. I submit, Mr. Chairman, this is far from being a parliamentary doctrine; I think it is an enunciation of an anti-parliamentary doctrine. This parliament, surely, is a court of appeal with respect to any matter, any problem, that lies within the whole scope of federal jurisdiction in this country. Any problem that arises surely ought to be able to find its way for discussion at some time or another on to the floor of the House of Commons. And for my part, Mr. Chairman, I reject completely the doctrine that the Prime Minister enunciated yesterday that parliament has no right to sit as a court of appeal when objection is taken to the exercise by the Bank of Canada of its powers in any particular way. If Canadians feel that those powers have been exercised in any way that they disapprove of, then, surely, this parliament is the forum before which they ought to be able to bring their complaints. That is the view that we of Her Majesty's loyal opposition take. We repel, we reject, the doctrine enunciated by the Prime Minister in this regard.
Now, sir, a question has arisen very directly as to the extent to which the government has participated in, or bears any responsibility for, the decision made by the Bank of Canada with respect to increases in the interest rate. In this respect, I think the Minister of Finance has been hiding behind a smokescreen of his own creation. He admits that he takes advice from the bank, he admits that he is made aware in advance of the course the bank takes. He said yesterday at page 7351 of Hansard, concerning the last increase by the Bank of Canada in the interest rate:
I was advised of this course before it was taken.
But then, having said that, the minister asks the house, in effect, to believe that he has no responsibility for what the bank does. Now, Mr. Chairman, he said on the same page yesterday:
This action is the action of the governor of the bank and his responsibility alone.

If that is true at all, Mr. Chairman, it is true only in the narrowest and most technical sense. The minister has a very direct responsibility because the action taken by the Bank of Canada in this respect surely has a direct influence on the whole field of action and on the whole field of responsibility of the government in relation to fiscal matters.
Take the situation in England. One does not find there the chancellor of the exchequer withdrawing himself from this issue when the Bank of England takes steps to raise the interest rate. You do not find him saying: I have no responsibility for this; this is the action of the Bank of England. It happens to be a bank whose stock is fully owned by the government, but do not hold the government responsible. You do not have the government there taking an irresponsible attitude of that kind.
Now, sir, it may originally have been intended, when the Bank of Canada was established in this country, that it should have some measure of independence of direct government fiscal action. Under the original set-up of the bank one-half of the bank stock was held in small lots by the public and one-half was held by the government. After the King government came into office in 1935 it took steps to expropriate the half of the issue of stock of the bank which was held in the hands of the public, and from that time on the government has owned all of the stock of the Bank of Canada.
I say, sir, that the government cannot shed its responsibility for full fiscal policy in the broadest sense of the word, and that must include the actions of the Bank of Canada, even when, in a technical sense, those actions are taken by the governor of the Bank of Canada in the exercise of the powers conferred upon him by the Bank of Canada Act. We ask the Minister of Finance now to say, and to say for the first time, because he has not said it yet, did not say it in his speech today, and has not said it at any time yet, whether he approves the actions taken by the Bank of Canada in those various stages, both with respect to the rate of interest and also with respect to restriction of credit in other forms. Let him say whether he did approve of those actions before they were taken by the Bank of Canada.
Now, sir, let me come specifically to these actions because I wish to be fair about this. I am not overlooking the realities of the situation, the dangers that exist or the responsibilities that are carried by those who sit opposite. The first series of actions taken by the Bank of Canada that I wish to speak
Supply-Finance
of was to make changes in the interest rate. There have been actually six changes made in the interest rate by the Bank of Canada in the past year and a half. The first was taken on February 1, 1955. At that time the bank lowered the interest rate from 2 per cent to 1J per cent. On August 5, 1955 the bank reversed that policy and raised the interest rate from lj per cent to 2 per cent. It followed this again on October 12 with a second increase, this time from 2 per cent to 2J per cent. On November 18 it raised the rate from 2\ per cent to 2J per cent. On April 4 of this year it introduced the fourth increase, this time from 2| per cent to 3 per cent-a record-and then this latest increase on August 9 from 3 to 3J per cent.
The inevitable effect of these actions has been that money becomes costly and every time an action of this kind is taken by the government with the consequent increase in interest it means the loss by bondholders of thousands-yes, and oftentimes millions-of dollars in the market value of their bonds, including the bond obligations issued by this government.
Every action of this kind has a disturbing effect. Whatever may be said about the case for taking such an action it cannot be denied that every time an action like this is taken it has a disturbing effect upon the financial market and upon public confidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It also has reassuring effect.

I have not yet argued the whole case with regard to this matter but I do wish to stress that every one of these actions has a disturbing effect of this nature.
The second type of action taken by the Bank of Canada was that it required the chartered banks to increase their ratio of liquid assets to a minimum of 15 per cent.
The Bank of Canada in its report for the year 1955 states at page 16:
After discussion, the banks have agreed to work to achieve by May 31, 1956, a minimum liquid asset ratio of 15 per cent which they will endeavour to maintain on a daily average basis from June on.
The effect of that increase in the minimum ratio of liquid assets of the chartered banks was, of course, to restrict commercial credit* In the course of conferences and communications between the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks the chartered banks were asked to curtail commercial loans. We had evidence to that effect from Mr. Nicks, the president of the Canadian Bankers Association, before the banking and commerce committee a week ago yesterday. The chartered banks complied with that request from the Bank of Canada. The result has been a severe curtailment of credit on the part of the banks.

Supply-Finance
Now, why has this course of action been taken? Why has this result been risked by the Bank of Canada and by the government? We have not' yet been given a very clear answer to that question even after waiting until today for the statement of the Minister of Finance. Was this done because of the fear or the threat of inflation? The Minister of Finance is very chary about the use of that word "inflation". I commented on this when speaking in the budget debate on March 27 last that the Minister of Finance in his budget speech had found himself very unwilling to mention the word "inflation".
The government has not yet told us that this action has been taken because of the existence of inflationary forces. The minister's statement today was anything but lucid on that point. The government knows the reason, but the minister has not chosen to make the reason clear to the house. At least the Prime Minister stated yesterday that the reason had been disclosed to the government. He said as reported at page 7352 of Hansard:
. . . I can assure the hon. gentleman that the matter received very serious consideration . . .
That was on the part of the government and we were told that the government knew the reason. Well, it certainly has not been made clear here.
Mr. Chairman, if one looks at what the Bank of Canada had to say in announcing on August 9 the reason for this fifth increase in the interest rate in the past year, one finds the reason put down by the bank was quite different from that to be drawn with some difficulty from the statement made by the minister today. The Canadian press dispatch which appeared following the announcement of the increase contains these words:
A government official said the increase reflects the fact that interest rates both in Canada and the United States are climbing. The increase was in line with this trend.
We are not told the identity of this mysterious government official who made the statement, but the statement he made certainly was not confirmed by the minister 1;oday. It would have been an understandable reason to give because admittedly interest rates have risen both in the United States and Great Britain. As a matter of fact, interest rates have been raised in Great Britain to record heights. Hon. members will recall that in February the interest rate was raised to 5| per cent. The reason plainly given at that time for the increase was that it was taken to curb extravagant spending and to meet the trend of inflation, and it was recognized that it would probably mean a rate

of 6J per cent on bank commercial loans. However, we are not given frank statements of that kind here.
The minister has carefully skirted this question. While we may regret that we have not been given clear statements by the minister in this regard I am going to assume for the purpose of a few comments that there is in the mind of the Bank of Canada and in the mind of the minister a fear of inflation. I do not believe for one minute that the Bank of Canada would act in a vacuum. We all have respect for the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. J. E. Coyne; he is a very serious man who takes a conscientious and grave view of his responsibilities.
The bank must have had some reason for this action. The reason given by the government official who was the spokesman on the occasion of the increase was that interest rates here should rise because they had risen in the United States and Great Britain. If the minister would state the problem and tell us specifically how he relates the various steps that have been proposed either by himself or the Bank of Canada or both, we would have an opportunity then of relating those steps and judging the efficacy of them in relation to the problem that the minister recognizes and presumably is trying to cope with, but he does not do that.
Let me say this about inflation, sir. We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition look upon inflation as a peril to be avoided at all times. We have not forgotten the ugly results of the period of postwar runaway inflation, particularly in the period after the outbreak of hostilities in Korea. We then had to plead in this house because of the effect it had on those on fixed incomes, pensioners and others and the disturbance of the economy in every sector which came about by reason of runaway inflation.
The difficulty with the kind of measures the government has taken here is that they have an indiscriminative effect. The president of the Royal Bank of Canada, Mr. James Muir, made an interesting comment in a speech early this year in relation to the type of policy of credit restriction which is reflected in these increases in the Bank of Canada rate. He said:
Experience shows that monetary policy is more effective against inflation than against deflation. But there are dangers. As I have already pointed out, the policy may go too far. It may also be unselective, curbing healthy as well as unhealthy or excessive bank credit.
The great difficulty about the kind of government action which has been taken here is that it has an indiscriminate application.

In the language of Mr. Muir, it has been "unselective, curbing healthy as well as unhealthy or excessive bank credit". Look at its effect on housing. The restriction of credit with respect to housing applied across the board, and I think it may fairly be said that its effects are being felt most by those engaged in the construction of small homes. There has not been any attempt to work out any policy of restriction of credit on a selective basis in order to provide needed credit for those engaged in the construction of small homes. Let some of the luxury apartment construction wait for a while, in favour of small houses, but no, this kind of policy of credit restriction has been applied indiscriminately.
Similarly in connection with commercial credit the generality of the application of this restrictive policy has denied business expansion in quarters where the expansion of business, had it been permitted, would have been an antidote to the inflationary forces which the minister sees at work.
When one is looking for evidence of inflation one normally turns to the cost of living. Thank goodness the statistics we have in relation to the consumer price index are somewhat reassuring in this respect, because, looking at page 24 of the July issue of the Canadian statistical review published by the dominion bureau of statistics, we see that in June, the last month available, the index stood at 117-8, which is a trifle higher than it has been but which compares, for instance, with August, 1954, when it stood at 117-0.
Good management by the Liberal government.

No, it is not good management by the Liberal government. That is a silly intrusion by the Minister of Fisheries, who will never leave it to his colleagues but who has to air his own views on other departments. It is not good management, unless it is good management to have the kind of situation arise that has resulted in the government apparently taking steps to restrict credit for many people who have justifiable claims for credit. The government takes all credit but-
The Liberal government-

If the minister would just restrain his volubility, perhaps he had better wait his turn. If he is going to insist on talking and using up my time I shall be obliged to ask you to give me additional time, Mr. Chairman.
The food index for June stands at 112-5 which compares with 113-7 for September, 1955 and September, 1954 figure of 113-8.
Supply-Finance
Shelter for June this year was 132-6, which is higher, having slowly come up somewhat rather steadily of late. Clothing has been quite constant. Other commodities and services stand at 120-6 for June, which is slightly higher than it was a year ago.
I think the figures on consumer purchasing are indicative of the steady rise in credit over a long period. I do not propose to put too many of these figures before the committee, but in the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada for 1955 we find at page 59 a record of the steady increase in consumer credit in this country, starting in 1948. Charge accounts in 1948 stood at $166 million, rising to $374 million by December 31, 1955. Retail dealers' instalment credit started at $81 million in 1948 and rose to $377 million at the end of 1955. Instalment credit through finance and loan companies started at $52 million in 1948 and rose steadily to $601 million at the end of 1955. Cash personal loans started in that period at $238 million and at the end of 1955 had risen to $830 million. The total of selected items in 1948 was $537 million, but at the end of 1955 had risen to $2,182 million. There has been a steady increase in consumer credit in this country, but there is no indication that this was a factor which led the government or the Bank of Canada into taking this action.
The July statistical review issued by the dominion bureau of statistics shows that in the last four years retail sales have increased rapidly, but the proportion of credit sales to the total has not risen. I do not wish to delay the committee unduly on this point, but I say that the figures show that cash sales have risen in amount but not in percentage of total sales, and that while credit sales have risen in amount, they have not risen in percentage of total retail sales.
If it is the threat of inflation which has led the government and the Bank of Canada to this series of actions then I suggest that there are responsibilities falling directly upon the government. Let the government begin at home. Let the government clean its own house. Let it look at its own swollen expenditures which represent one of the biggest and strongest inflationary factors in our economy today. At one point the minister almost admitted that. If the government would look around for ways and means of restraining inflationary factors I submit that it first ought to pluck the beam out of its own eye.
Hon. members should not forget that inflationary factors oftentimes have the subtle support of and exercise a siren attraction upon ministers of finance because the government always shares through the tax

Supply-Finance
impositions in the benefits of inflation, through swollen returns of income tax, corporation tax, sales tax and other impositions.
The effect of these repeated increases in interest rates, five in a period of one year, has been a tremendous increase in the burdens cast upon provincial governments with respect to their borrowings and upon municipal governments with respect to their borrowings, and upon business, and punishing losses upon the holders of Canada's obligations. What the government should be directing its efforts toward in facing the threat of inflation is to seek an increase in productivity.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman but it is my duty to inform him that his time has expired.
I had reached the last sentence.
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: With the consent of the committee the hon. member may continue.
I should like to hear the hon. member finish.
Agreed.

This is my last sentence. I think that a good deal of the solution lies within the power of the government. On the one hand we have the government lauding the boom and asking political support because they claim we have a buoyant economy with expanding revenues, and on the other hand we have the government taking steps which look as though they were trying to apply the brakes and put a check on the very things for which they are claiming political credit. Let them stop applying conflicting and contradictory policies.

The hon. member for Eglinton has taken the Minister of Finance to task for not having said in so many words in his statement that he approved of this increase in the interest rate by the Bank of Canada. The mystery seems to be whether the hon. member for Eglinton approves it or not because he has not told us. I must point out, however, that the change in the Bank of Canada rate is to a very large extent hardly more than an indicator, not having any really direct effect in the way of raising interest rates in other fields, as can be seen from the statistics published by the Bank of Canada in this financial supplement for 1955, in which you see that the highest amount of loans from the Bank of
(Mr. Fleming.)
Canada to the chartered banks was $15 million and that by the end of the year that was only $2 million.
The hon. member for Eglinton quoted some government officials as saying that this change in the Bank of Canada's rate was merely a reflection of changes in other places, and I think that is true. Much more effective are other actions of the Bank of Canada, and those are the actions that were outlined to us by the governor when he appeared before the banking and commerce committee, in which he told us of the agreement which had been reached with the chartered banks to achieve a certain ratio of liquidity in their assets which they were hopeful of being able to achieve shortly after the agreement was reached, and the other perhaps less formal agreement to curtail term loans from the chartered banks.
That there is a necessity for curbing in some way some of the tendencies in our economy at the present time I think will be revealed clearly by the figures issued by the Bank of Canada, figures which the hon. member for Eglinton put on the record of the banking and commerce committee last week.
Those are the same ones to which I referred this afternoon.

Yes. They clearly indicate the necessity for some sort of action, whether or not one agrees with the action taken or whether or not one agrees it is an effective action. The increase in the consumer credit from March 31, 1954, to March 31, 1956, shows that the trend is accelerated. From March 1954 to March 1955 there was an increase of $109 million, but in the next year, March 1955 to March 1956, there was an increase in certain selected items, as they were called, of $352 million. When we compare that with the figures for increase in labour income for approximately the same period, we can see that there is something very dangerous in our economy.
I am sorry that I have not been able to compare it with the same dates, but the statistics do not allow that. From May 1955, . from $637 million of labour income, the increase to May this year was only to $676 million, some $39 million. Those two sets of figures compared show that at least in one sector of our economy we are entering very dangerous grounds, but perhaps more dangerous still is the field to which the minister made reference in his remarks earlier this afternoon. That is the field of general bank credit issued in those periods.
I see from the Bank of Canada's report that the total of bank loans in January 1954 was $4,096 million, and in January 1955 there

was actually less, $4,050 million, whereas from January 1955 to January 1956 there was a climb to $4,884 million, or an increase of $834 million, some 20 per cent. When we take the increases after that period, for the rest of this year, we see them climbing even more rapidly, so I think there is perfectly plain evidence that some action ought to be taken by the financial and monetary authorities of this country.
I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton that there are certain weaknesses in the method used. I am not sure that other methods could have been used, but certainly those that have been used have been inevitably used in an indiscriminatory manner so that we have the general curtailment of credit all across the field. Where in many instances it might be certainly to our social advantage to have it curtailed, there may be other areas in which it may not well have been increased. That, of course, is the inevitable result of the set-up of our financial institutions in Canada.
There is, of course, another method that the Bank of Canada uses on occasion to attempt to curb such a period as we appear to be going into. Mr. Coyne told us in the banking and commerce committee that it was, by and large, the most effective method, apart from consultation with the chartered banks; and that is, of course, the method of open market operations. However, he denied the suggestion of some of us on the committee that there was inevitable conflict in the purposes of the bank in open market operations, a conflict between the aim of curtailing inflation and reducing total money supply and the position of government bonds, that that conflict was always there and largely hamstrings the bank when it attempts to deal with the situation by that method.
I would suggest that sooner or later in Canada we are going to have to take some very drastic steps with regard to the channeling of investment in this country. We have all observed the attempts by the government to channel investment into the fields that they think are socially and economically desirable. We have seen the rather desperate efforts to channel it into housing and the various roadblocks they have met in different places, because in the last analysis this government and this parliament has no control over the fields of investment in which those who have control of pools of capital place their funds.
I suggest that the step that was taken- and, I gather, rather deplored by the hon. member for Eglinton-with regard to the Bank of Canada is a step which eventually they are going to have to take with regard
Supply-Finance
to the whole of the banking system of Canada. We cannot any more say that it is feasible to operate the central bank on a part publicly owned and a part privately owned basis. Sooner or later we are going to have to face the facts that the chartered banks and the central bank are parts of one integrated monetary and financial system and that they also must be placed under one control and under one policy. It is useless charging the chartered banks, as I have heard them charged in recent days, with failing in their social duty, because they also have a conflict in duties. When I hear members, as I have heard them, charging the chartered banks with having failed dismally in entering into the necessary field of consumer credit, I am rather astonished, because those same hon. members would be the very first to object were it proposed that the public authority should tell some of the privately owned institutions what particular business it should engage in, which particular line it should drop and which particular line it should continue.
We can only expect that those who are responsible to shareholders of private institutions, such as the chartered banks, are bound-in fact, it is their duty-to maximize as well as possible the returns to the shareholders of those institutions.
I suggest that we are going to have these conflicts, we are going to have these rather ineffective attempts to control inflation in our economy, so long as we have this rather anomalous situation of an important, perhaps the most important, part of our monetary system and our financial institutions, held in private hands by people whose interests are bound inevitably on occasion to conflict with the public interest. But I for one am very glad that the Bank of Canada has taken this action. I am doubtful as to whether it will be very effective, but it certainly is a warning to the country of the great dangers that lie ahead, a warning that we all ought to heed very carefully. Whilst these increases in total bank loans may not yet, as the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out, have caused any increase in the cost of living, by the time they are realized in investment we may very well be facing a very severe rise in the cost of living and very dangerous inflationary tendencies.
My complaint would be that the Bank of Canada delayed too long in this action and allowed the situation to get too far out of hand before attempting to curb it.

Mr. Chairman, we Social Creditors are not desirous of participating in the discussion of this particular item until we have heard what the other members

Supply-Finance
have to say. I think there are some other hon. members who desire to speak.

Before we go on with the other items, there are one or two things I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. Each time there has been an increase in the central bank rate of interest the accompanying news item in the paper always says this is done to prevent inflation. According to the New Brunswick brief the situation is this; and I think the growers in New Brunswick, possibly even more so than those on the island, are in an awkward position because we have to move our potatoes by rail, and freight rates are not quite so favourable there. Also owing to the fact that, from the point of view of the return from a cash crop, we produce close to 20 per cent of all the potatoes grown in Canada, I think these people down there understand the situation fairly well.
As I understand it, their requests may be a little bit different, and I think possibly this is what the minister was referring to. They first said, "We would be quite willing to have no duty at all, to have free passage back and forward across the international boundary". I am sure they feel that would be the best way. Nevertheless they realize that such a thing could only be brought about by negotiation and by this government being able to convince the United States government that their potato industry would not be injured in any particular manner. In other words it would be the United States government that would have to take off their duty.
Realizing that this would be possibly quite difficult to bring about, at least without some bargaining method, their second and strongest recommendation up to the present was that until such time as the situation expressed in No. 1, to which I have just referred, was brought about, there should be a countervailing duty of 37 J cents at all times on potatoes entering Canada from the United States.
The point is this, that when the minister's statement is read by our potato growers they are going to take a far different view of it than perhaps the minister intended. I am not going to go into this in detail at all because I do not want to delay the house. I do not think I can be accused of delaying these estimates, and I do not want to be guilty of that at this stage. The minister did make a statement at page 7108 of Hansard, and I do not want to repeat the whole of it. There is this line:
Supply-Finance
However, there may be other means whereby we can meet the requests of the potato producers at least to some extent.
The minister has said it would not be possible to induce the United States government to change its tariff in accordance with the wishes of the potato growers, and I would say he meant in accordance with the wishes expressed in paragraph 1 of the New Brunswick submission. Since the minister made no statement today, and possibly intended that to be a statement in answer to my question the other day, I am wondering if he will not enlighten the house and the people across Canada who are interested in producing potatoes as to just what the government had in mind when he made the statement that there may be other means whereby the requests of the potato growers could be met.
The minister went on a few lines later to say that this matter is not very pressing though it may be on future occasions. Let me be very fair about it. I think that conveys to the potato growers of this country that they are not getting the consideration they feel they should be getting. If the minister had not qualified that statement the farmers would have been led to believe there was something being considered and an announcement might have been made before September 1, when the crop commences to move. If there is any announcement the minister can make I should like him to tell us what is being considered, so the growers will know before they start moving their crops.
Last year, for instance, the crop commenced to move in September, and farmer after farmer was forced to sell when the market was lowest in order to get money. Many of them had to sell at half the cost of production. During the first four months of the movement they were trying to get negotiations under way with the Department of Agriculture because they thought that was the proper department to approach in order to get some sort of program that would give some stability to the crop. When that did come the program did give some stability, though it came far too late for many producers who took heavy losses. Nevertheless the program not only stabilized the market, but from that time on the market commenced to go up.
There is one more thing the tariff board report does not mention. I do not know whether or not it was in the presentation, but it does affect the economy of the potato producer. Until last year Canada grade 1 potatoes measured two inches. This was changed in order to meet the competition from across the border. The state of Maine, one state in the United States, raised the size of their grade 1 potato; and according to federal law when

Supply-Finance
any state took such action affecting the grade of potatoes it became effective in all states, so we were obliged to do something to keep the smaller sized potatoes, which would be considered culls by our potato growers, from going into the market as Canada grade 1.
I do not think there is too much criticism of that change, but remember when that action was taken our farmers then faced a larger number of culls. It is true that a potato anywhere from an inch and a half to two inches is a good table potato, but it is not accepted as Canada grade 1. This means that if a farmer has a large crop of potatoes, in some yields he gets a good many that are under two and a half inches and which are good eating potatoes, but he cannot market them as Canada grade 1. He must feed them to his stock or turn them over to a starch factory if there is one within an economic distance from him.
All these things affect the farmers position. The cost of machinery and the capital outlay to raise a crop of potatoes will be just as great if a lot of them are culls as it will be if a greater number of them are Canada grade 1. I think it is as the result of a lot of things like this that the matter is pressing, and I think the potato growers are entitled to know what the government has in mind.
There is something else that has affected us down east which does not affect some of the provinces, and that is the freight rate change. You may be surprised to know-
